title: Persistent to the End
core: All of these describe someone who keeps going: effort sustained past the point where a normal person would stop, in the face of difficulty, tedium, or discouragement. They differ on three axes the GRE cares about. First, whether the speaker approves — most are praise, one is a complaint. Second, what the persistence pushes against: opposition and failure, physical tiredness, or the sheer grind of detail. Third, what the word attaches to — a person's character, a long campaign, or an inanimate nuisance that will not go away.

words.nuance: The plain-English, working-class member of the group — no polish, no grandeur. It praises the unglamorous grunt: the one still knocking on doors in month nine, not the one who solved it cleverly. Where the others are formal, **dogged** is the word you'd actually say out loud, and it implies the work was boring as well as hard.

The only insult here. **Pertinacious** tells you the speaker wants this to stop — the grip is aimed at something not worth gripping, and it has outlasted everyone's patience. It's also the one that attaches comfortably to non-persons: a pertinacious cough, a pertinacious rumour, a pertinacious creditor. Nobody claims it about themselves.

Alone in the group, this names what's *absent* — fatigue — rather than the obstacle overcome. There need be no adversity at all; the marvel is the sheer un-tiring output, sustained over years by a campaigner or advocate. It's the grandest compliment on the list, and slightly hyperbolic: literally, cannot be worn out.

The only one about **care**, not endurance against resistance. What a sedulous person outlasts is the tedium of detail — every footnote checked, every entry verified — and the praise is for thoroughness, never for defying opposition. Unhurried where *industrious* is energetic; you can be sedulous at a task nobody is fighting you over.

The group's only noun, and the one that requires actual setback: **perseverance** presumes you already failed, were discouraged, and kept going anyway. Take away the obstacle and the word has nothing to describe. It names the virtue abstractly — the quality itself, awarded credit — rather than characterizing a person the way the adjectives do.

exam_note: The trap is tonal: **pertinacious** looks like a fancy upgrade of *dogged* or *tenacious*, so it gets slotted into admiring sentences where only a negative word fits — check for a "though/regrettably" signal or an exasperated speaker before choosing it.
